To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) girls whose mothers were younger at the birth of their first child tend to mature early; 2) girls whose mothers have a history of depression tend to mature early (but this effect is mediated by the mother’s age at the birth of her first child); 3) girls whose mothers report high levels of family conflict tend to mature early, especially if the mother is younger at the birth her first child; 4) girls whose mothers are more controlling tend to mature early and

(a) the earlier a girl is exposed to her father, the earlier she is likely to begin puberty, (b) the earlier a mother is exposed to her own mother, the earlier her daughter is likely to begin pubertal development, (c) the more positive the mother-daughter relationship, the later a girl is likely to begin menstruating and (d) the more positive her relationship with her father, the later a daughter is likely to experience menarche.

(i) girls who experienced high quality parenting in early life tend to mature earlier than their peers; (ii) girls who experienced low quality parenting in early childhood tend to mature later than their peers; and (iii) girls who experienced early childhood adversity tend to mature later, but only in contexts characterized by high quality parenting.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the proximate and ultimate causes of variation in pubertal timing.
the effects of family environment on reproductive strategies and the timing of puberty.
the ways in which early family experiences shape reproductive strategies and how these experiences may be linked to the timing of pubertal maturation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
early family experience affects the timing of pubertal onset, which in turn affects reproductive strategy.
the timing of female pubertal onset is influenced by a number of factors including genetic and environmental influences.
early family experience, including parental investment in offspring, has a significant effect on the timing of female puberty.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pubertal timing and reproductive strategy are both influenced by early experience and that the two developmental trajectories may be linked.
the quality of the mother-infant bond is a key determinant of the timing of pubertal maturation.
early family experience affects the timing and tempo of pubertal development, with consequences for reproductive strategy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
pubertal timing and reproductive strategies are not fixed at conception, but are shaped by experiences in the family.
early family experience matters for reproductive strategy.
early family experience is a potent determinant of female pubertal development and, as a consequence, of the timing of the transition to sexual maturity.
